newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Rebel Tajik colonel to step down, withdraw troops.
newsitem.headline: Rebel Tajik colonel to step down, withdraw troops.

text.p: Rebel Tajik Colonel Makhmud Khudoyberdyev has agreed to step down as commander of his elite brigade and to withdraw his troops to barracks after talks with President Imomali Rakhmonov, a presidential spokesman said on Wednesday.
"Khudoyberdyev has resigned as commander of his brigade and will work in another post," Zafar Saidov told Reuters.
"All questions between both sides have been resolved on peaceful lines. Makhmud Khudoyberdyev agreed without any conditions to move all his forces back to barrcks."
Saidov said Khudoyberdyev had made the concessions during two telephone conversations with Rakhmonov. He said the two men did not meet personally.
Earlier on Wednesday, Russian news agencies said Rakhmonov and Khudoyberdyev had begun talks at a Russian peacekeepers' base in the capital Dushanbe.
"Later today the president will issue a decree removing Makhmud Khudoyberdyev from his command, appointing him to another post," Saidov said.
All forces loyal to the mutinous colonel have moved back to their base in the southern town of Kurgan Tyube, he said.

The colonel's headquarters in Kurgan Tyube, about 110 km (70 miles) south of Dushanbe, contacted by telephone, declined comment. Forces loyal to Rakhmonov have been battling the renegade colonel since Saturday.
Khudoyberdyev, 34, the politically ambitious commander of an elite government armoured brigade, has mutinied twice before in as many years.
He has also been a vociferous critic of a peace deal Rakhmonov signed in June with the republic's armed Islamic opposition aimed at ending four years of civil war.
He moved his armour towards Dushanbe at the weekend after fighting broke out between two rival warlords in the capital but his motives for doing so are unclear.
Khudoyberdyev said on Tuesday he had no plans to take the capital and said he had been provoked by what he said was the presidential guard's move on his territory in the south.
He lost control of a strategically important aluminium smelter west of the capital to the presidential guard on Monday.
